claims.text: The proposed initial material is a single-phase BCC refractory alloy such as W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf or HfNbTaTiZr.
At sufficiently high temperature, the initial alloy is a disordered solid solution with negligible SRO.
Cr-Hf and Cr-V interactions have strong negative mixing tendencies that promote chemical ordering.
Isothermal annealing at 600–1000 K will nucleate and grow SRO clusters.
Cr-Hf attraction facilitates coalescence of SRO clusters.
Cr-Hf chemical order is nonzero below its order-disorder transition and vanishes near 1080 K in the cited W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf composition.
The proposed regime excludes long-range phase separation and precipitation and retains a single BCC phase.
SRO clusters coalesce into a connected network spanning the grain or simulation cell.
Isolated SRO clusters act as phonon-scattering centers and reduce thermal conductivity.
Percolating ordered domains can facilitate coherent phonon propagation and thereby reduce scattering.
Percolating SRO can alter the phonon density of states in a way that counteracts SRO-induced scattering.
Percolating SRO produces a nonlinear thermal-conductivity transition, potentially yielding a plateau or increase.
Thermal conductivity will show non-monotonic behavior or an inflection point at the SRO percolation threshold.
Serial or parallel mixing models and simple scattering models predict a continuous monotonic conductivity reduction proportional to SRO-cluster volume fraction.
The hypothesis is restricted to alloys in which SRO reaches percolation without evolving into distinct precipitates.
Standard interatomic potentials may predict the wrong SRO evolution or cluster morphology.
The predicted transition point and conductivity deviation depend on the potential energy surface accurately representing SRO evolution.

Simultaneous conductivity, Warren-Cowley SRO, cluster-connectivity, and optional phonon-density-of-states measurements are proposed to test temporal coincidence between percolation and the conductivity anomaly.
A monotonic conductivity decrease with increasing SRO, no percolation-associated anomaly, and agreement with a standard scattering model within experimental error would falsify the hypothesis.
